<h2>Hanover</h2>



<p><a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://kestnergesellschaft.de/en/exhibition/112" target="_blank">Karimah Ashadu: <em>Crystalline</em></a></p>



<p>The British-born Nigerian artist Karimah Ashadu’s filmmaking operates on two levels of specificity: in documenting the material conditions and lived circumstances of contemporary Nigeria – its informal economies and cultural idiosyncrasies; and in the thematics of her images, with camerawork sculpting the masculine body (<em>MUSCLE</em>, 2025) or swivelling across an outdoor abattoir like a filleting knife (<em>King of Boys</em> <em>[Abattoir of Makoko]</em>, 2015). Bodies, meat, markets, economies. There’s referential play to be had, too, be it the psychodramas of the western genre nodded to in <em>Cowboy</em> (2022) or <em>MUSCLE</em>’s ogling editing cadence. <em>Crystalline</em> will premiere Ashadu’s new film <em>WAVES</em>, set in a ‘makeshift car wash in Lagos, run by young men displaced from northern Nigeria by political conflict’, shown in tandem with photographs, sculpture and <em>Cowboy</em>. Exhibitions in Chicago of Ashadu’s back catalogue, <em>Tendered</em> at Renaissance Society and <em>Machine Boys</em> at Art Institute of Chicago, follow hot on <em>Crystalline</em>’s heels in September. Watch closely. <em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/alexander-leissle/">Alexander Leissle</a></em></p>



<p><em>Kestner Gesellschaft, 29 August – 15 November</em></p>

<h2>Boston</h2>



<p><a href="https://www.icaboston.org/exhibitions/leilah-babirye/">Leilah Babirye: <em>Embaga ya Naki ne Naki (Wedding of Naki and Naki)</em> </a></p>



<p>When Leilah Babirye moved to New York after being outed in Uganda – where she was born and where homosexuality is illegal – she made money by recycling cans, babysitting and delivering for Uber Eats. Even looking at these temporary jobs, one can tease out the preoccupations of her art practice: salvage, care, a particular penchant for bicycle gears and chains. Made from wood or clay and outfitted with rubber scraps and junk metal, Babirye’s anthropomorphic statues and busts honour real people ranging from royal figures to her friends and chosen family. The selection that will go on view in Boston – following recent presentations at the de Young Museum in San Francisco and the 2024 Venice Biennale – extends Babirye’s interest in queer Black kinship and love. The glazed ceramic sculpture <em>Tuli Mukwano (We Are in Love) III</em> (2025) sits at the heart of the show, which is staged as a wedding for a genderless couple who share the name Naki. Here, two pocked and somnambulant heads, adorned with a metal hose and rubber tubing, meet at an angle. Mouths, smeared red, strain towards one another without touching. The newlyweds’ ragged dignity radiates through the fictional ceremony. Among Babirye’s sculptures one finds that, as John Berger once wrote of Brâncuși’s stone <em>Kisses</em>, ‘Not one is polished and not one is platonic.’ <em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/jenny-wu/">Jenny Wu</a></em></p>



<p><em>ICA Boston, 27 August – 18 January 2027</em></p>

<h2>New Plymouth</h2>



<p><a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://govettbrewster.com/exhibitions/2026/economies-of-deferral" target="_blank"><em>Economies of Deferral</em></a></p>



<p>Fiona Clark is best known for the social documentary photographs she began making during the 1970s among Auckland’s queer and trans communities, preserving in these images lives and forms of self-expression that were largely excluded from Aotearoa New Zealand’s public record. Across five decades, she has treated photography as a form of witnessing, working closely with the people she depicts while documenting their health struggles, Indigenous rights issues (her series <em>Te Iwi o Te Wāhi Kore</em>, made between 1979 and 1982, which confronted the seizure and subsequent pollution of iwi land along the Mount Taranaki coastline, became a significant political tool in the assertion of iwi land rights) and the environmental effects of extractive industry in Taranaki, where the artist lives.</p>



<p>Her latest performance, <em>What would this place look like without fossil fuel sponsorship?</em>, continues her inquiry into that last. Recorded in 2025, the performance, which sees Clark circle the Len Lye Centre before dawn, dressed in repurposed hessian sacks while staring into its mirrored steel facade, draws attention to what cultural spaces conceal when they accept funding from industries implicated in ecological damage, and what kind of economic systems these institutions rely on.</p>



<p>Clark’s performance is being screened as part of <em>Economies of Deferral</em>, a group exhibition examining how the consequences of political and industrial decisions are displaced across time, communities and landscapes. Bringing together work by Clark, Darcy Lange and John Miller, Matthew Galloway, Ngahuia Harrison and <a href="https://artreview.com/ho-rui-an-artspace-helutrans-singapore-review-adeline-chia/">Ho Rui An</a>, the exhibition traces the effects of economic and industrial change, from the unemployment caused by the market reforms of 1980s Aotearoa to oil extraction and its impact on the environment, refinery closures and the country’s dependence on global petroleum supply chains – tracing the gap between promises of prosperity and the unresolved costs they leave behind. <em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/fi-churchman/">Fi Churchman</a></em></p>



<p><em>Govett-Brewster Art Gallery</em>, <em>8 August – 15 November</em></p>

<h2>Nikko</h2>



<p><em><a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://troedssonvilla.org/lightinaugust/" target="_blank">Light in August</a></em></p>



<p>Organised by artists Anne Eastman and Tam Ochiai, and presented by Troedsson Villa Mountain School, this exhibition brings together a surprising constellation of US artists: Pope.L, Danny McDonald and Kiki Smith; and Japanese: Emi Otaguro, Miki Kubota, Tomomi Nishimura and others – in an over-a-century-old pawnbroker’s shop. Eastman and Ochiai’s graceful curating responds ingeniously, yet considerately, to the site, and the result is breezy. Inside, there is an <em>unryuzu</em>, or dragon and clouds painted on the ceiling, which came with the building. Outside, dragonflies take respite on Taichi Moriyama’s standout perches – each composed of a steel rod and found objects, such as stones and snail shells – that dot the garden. Kubota’s aslant and uncanny chair brings a corridor of Otaguro’s light-handed animal paintings to full stop. Events and workshops are to be held throughout the month with a revolving roster of artists in residence. In the late afternoon of my visit, strangers lay together on the tatami floor taking in a screening of a diaristic videowork by, and in remembrance of, the recently passed and much missed Hiroyuki Oki. <em><a href="https://jp.artreview.com/author/taronettleton/">Taro Nettleton</a></em></p>



<p><em>The Pawnbroker’s Museum, through 31 August</em></p>

<h2>Birmingham</h2>



<p><em><a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.birmingham.gov.uk/events/event/5516/discovering_lisel_haas_exhibition" target="_blank">Discovering Lisel Haas</a></em></p>



<p>Best-known as a photojournalist, Lisel Haas was forced to flee her native Mönchengladbach in 1938, following the events of Kristallnacht, the Nazi party’s violent pogrom against Jews. She ended up in Birmingham, England, together with her partner, Grete Bermbach, where she gained a permit to work as a photographer for The Birmingham Repertory Theatre before establishing a successful practice as a portrait photographer. Between the two she developed a body of work that captured stars and ordinary citizens alike. Since her death, her remarkable archive has been housed in the Library of Birmingham, and material from it will be exhibited in a new exhibition that promises to bring together ‘Jewish refugee history, lesbian history, women’s lives, exile, photography and Birmingham’s cultural memory’. Also on view will be the work of five contemporary artists responding to a legacy that in many ways was rendered invisible, largely as a result of the extent to which Haas’s extraordinary life was devoted to documenting the ordinary and the everyday. Moreover, in a time of heightened intolerance towards outsiders, it provides an important tribute to the ways in which refugees and migrants can enhance civic life. <em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/nirmala-devi/">Nirmala Devi</a></em></p>



<p><em>Library of Birmingham, through 12 December</em></p>

<h2>São Paulo</h2>



<p><a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DYucxDCll8u/?utm_source=ig_web_copy_link&amp;igsh=MzRlODBiNWFlZA==" target="_blank">Luisa Matsushita: <em>Everything I Know, I Learned at Night</em></a></p>



<p>For four years Aberto, a platform for travelling exhibitions, has provided manna for nosy Paulistanos, opening up modernist architectural masterpieces in the Brazilian megalopolis to the public and dressing them with twentieth-century and contemporary art. The first edition, in 2022 occupied the only residential project designed by Oscar Niemeyer in the city; in 2023 a 1974 Vilanova Artigas villa was filled, the swimming pool included, with works by over 70 artists; while for the 2024 edition curators Filipe Assis, Kiki Mazzucchelli and Claudia Moreira Salles sourced the homes Chu Ming Silveira and Tomie Ohtake had built for themselves (Silveira designing her own; Ohtake commissioning her son Ruy). Earlier this year it was the turn of the Sputnik-like Casa Bola by Eduardo Longo, but now Aberto is spinning out a series of solo exhibitions, the art again moving to a new beguiling location each time.&nbsp;</p>



<p>The first of these features painter Luísa Matsushita’s sweeping colour blocks on canvas occupying the Teatro Cultura Artística. When Rino Levi designed the downtown cultural venue in the 1950s his plans included a gallery, but the room was never used as such. Seventy years later, the architect’s vision will be inaugurated with Matsushita’s work, the artist’s emphasis on abstraction and palette finding ancestry both in Levi’s yellow interior walls, blue floors and green columns, but also the iconic modernist mural by Emiliano Di Cavalcanti that graces the facade of the theatre. Matsushita will also produce a 15-metre-wide installation for the theatre’s main lobby. <em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/oliver-basciano/">Oliver Basciano</a></em></p>

<h2>Seoul</h2>



<p><a href="https://www.mmca.go.kr/eng/exhibitions/exhibitionsDetail.do?exhFlag=1" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">Christine Sun Kim: <em>Have Many Dumb Fight Against Rock</em></a></p>



<p>As Christine Sun Kim’s midcareer retrospective is wrapping up at the Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, at the end of the month, following its <a href="https://artreview.com/christine-sun-kim-all-day-all-night-whitney-museum-of-american-art-new-york-review-maddie-hampton/">debut last year</a> at the Whitney in New York, the artist has embarked on a new site-specific commission for the MMCA’s ‘Seoul Box’, as part of the museum’s ongoing partnership with consumer electronic company LG. The exhibition extends Kim’s exploration of language as an imperfect system of communication, rooted in the artist’s experience as a Deaf woman. This work is composed of her characteristic black-and-white, comic book-inspired lines, here expressing motion (that of ASL hand gestures) and accompanied by text stating ‘Have Many Dumb Fight Against Rock’ in English and Korean. These illustrations and words have been turned into adhesive vinyls that cover the floors and walls of the gallery, and into animations on a massive, curved screen. With Kim’s usual humour, the work attempts to tackle the frustration of fruitless communication, when language is just a vehicle for unbudging ideologies – like in Youtube comment sections or when trying to get your deposit back from your landlord. Or like when conflict escalates into fullscale war. <em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/mia-stern/">Mia Stern</a></em></p>



<p><em>MMCA Seoul, through 29 November</em></p>

<h2>Sharjah</h2>



<p><a href="https://www.sharjahart.org/en/whats-on/details/vantage-point-13">Vantage Point 13</a></p>



<p>The 13th edition of Vantage Point will take place in Sharjah Art Foundation’s newly built Photography Gallery, whose 450-square-metre exhibition space, opened in January, is the latest add-on to the multi-venue art museum helmed by Hoor Al Qasimi. Like its previous iterations, this one is the result of an open call, featuring six artists who, unlike before, were each given a fund to produce a new body of work broadly exploring the ‘possibilities of documentary photography’. Maheder Haileselassie’s <em>Arbegnoych</em> series (2026), for example, examines the stories of Ethiopian resistance fighters during the Italian occupation of the country via identification portraiture, questioning the type of photographic truth that portraiture claims to reveal. Guanyu Xu’s&nbsp;ongoing <em>Resident Aliens </em>project (2020–) pictures the homes of those considered to be immigrants, exploring how images mediate memories and one’s sense of identity. There’s also Luisa Dörr, Latifa AlBokhari, Sathish Kumar and Adam Rouhana, whose works experiments with photography’s possibility as a communal medium, telling the story of community and belonging – themes that, in today’s world of constant crisis and wars, are still poignantly felt in the region. <em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/yuwen-jiang/">Yuwen Jiang</a></em></p>

<h2>New York</h2>



<p><a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.momaps1.org/en/programs/747-courtyard-commission-precious-okoyomon" target="_blank">Precious Okoyomon: <em>Among the Flowers I Learned to Love: A Garden of Decreation</em></a></p>



<p>Circumambulating Precious Okoyomon’s outdoor installation, like a monk around a stupa, one admires the blooming coneflowers, their raspberry-shaped disks; the mauve and sorbet-orange hummingbird mint; the glazed tiles embedded in the fresh soil. These are etched with naive drawings of the sun and oblique handwritten messages that call on viewers to ‘Construct an obstruction already weaponized within’ and ‘Keep falling into calculated fading’. To actually interact with the work – to go up the seven sandstone steps that deliver one into the raised anus of a hill-sized brown teddy bear splayed on its stomach (<em>The Pleasure Principle</em>, 2026) and down the slide inside its body that ends in the round chamber of its mouth – is the domain of children. Signs warn of low clearance; the slide itself is only about a metre long. Hence, the installation draws a dividing line, between those who contemplate and those who act, those who think seriously about play and those who embody it; and, per the central sculpture’s evocative title, the superego and the id, desire and its denial, and the irresolution of what Okoyomon has called ‘the creature within us’. <em><em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/jenny-wu/">Jenny Wu</a></em></em></p>



<p><em>MoMA PS1, through 2028 </em></p>

Courtesy the artist</figcaption></figure>



<h2>Amsterdam</h2>



<p><a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.hartwigproxy.nl/programme/sonsbeek-films" target="_blank">Sonsbeek 2026 x Hartwig Art Foundation: <em>The Curved Times of Memory (What Would I Do in Orbit)?</em></a></p>



<p>When not summoned by Buddhists or Nietzscheans, spiralling or curved conceptions of time are often associated with particular conceptions of ancestrality and memory, particularly those relating to Indigenous worldviews. All the rage in the artworld right now. This film programme takeover of Hartwig Proxy, organised as part of Arnhem’s – it’s in the Netherlands, not far from the border with Germany – Sonsbeek (which styles itself as one of the ‘oldest recurring public-art festival in Europe) bucks that trend, getting rid of any form of human agency entirely (sort of – there are still human artists involved). Instead, the programme looks at the notion of memory (and time) on a curving, escalating scale – from the body, to a landscape, to a planet. The programme features works by <a href="https://artreview.com/korakrit-arunanondchai-nostalgia-for-unity-bangkok-kunsthalle-review-max-crosbie-jones/">Korakrit Arunanondchai</a>, Anne-Mie Van Kerckhoven, Jota Mombaça and Larry Achiampong, each of whom is participating in Sonsbeek 2026, curated by<strong> </strong>Amira Gad and Christina Li. The film programme itself is directly inspired by Van Kerckhoven’s work, a flower carpet that looks to the Milky Way as a source of inspiration and the spiral as a healing force. But don’t get too caught up looking up when you should be looking forwards. There are two ‘live moments’ on the cards as well: ‘a weekend of <a href="https://www.mailinglijst.nl/redirect.aspx?l=2643876&amp;a=15036345&amp;t=H&amp;ls=115575&amp;ahash=1287BFB8B85A786EECF5B7BDAC79DB3D8CC336359839D5EB19DAF7DA0A4F4ABB&amp;lhash=EE1EECB1535505A6F5EA9460D468D73D4C4C054E98033B0A18E8109048BAC908">workshops</a> and performances on 5–6 September, including a <a href="https://www.mailinglijst.nl/redirect.aspx?l=2643877&amp;a=15036345&amp;t=H&amp;ls=115575&amp;ahash=1287BFB8B85A786EECF5B7BDAC79DB3D8CC336359839D5EB19DAF7DA0A4F4ABB&amp;lhash=1DF293BE6EB2C34AAB0A42F63AFE41C12C1C4915185415C96551C90B0E50C194">bus ride</a> leaving from Proxy in Amsterdam to Arnhem, and a closing gathering on 13 October’. <em><a href="https://artreview.com/author/nirmala-devi/">Nirmala Devi</a></em></p>

<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Flavia_foto_28-6-17-002.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-126064" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Flavia_foto_28-6-17-002.jpg 1000w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Flavia_foto_28-6-17-002-600x899.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Flavia_foto_28-6-17-002-300x449.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Flavia_foto_28-6-17-002-768x1150.jpg 768w" sizes="(max-width: 1000px) 100vw, 1000px" /><figcaption>Courtesy MASP</figcaption></figure>



<p>Flávia Almeida, currently vice president of MASP (the São Paulo Museum of Art), is to become the Brazilian institution’s president. She takes over from Heitor Martins who, after 12 years at the helm, will depart in September. </p>



<p>Almeida comes from a business and management background. She holds a business administration degree from Fundação Getúlio Vargas and an MBA from Harvard University. Formerly she was the director of Fundação Bienal de São Paulo, where she still sits on the board, and chair of the board at São Paulo’s Instituto Tomie Ohtake. She has served as the president and board member of an array of publicly traded and privately held companies, including until 2003 at McKinsey &amp; Company (where Martins is also a partner).</p>



<p>Almeida joins a MASP revamped under Martins’s lead. In 2014 the institution was facing bankruptcy with r$75 million in debt, as well as serious issues ranging from power outages to theft of artworks from its collection. Martins raised r$1.5 billion worth of investment, and built a r$30 million reserve. A further r$275 million was raised to build the 14-story extension, Edifício Pietro Maria Bardi, which opened in March last year.</p>



<p>In 2014 Adriano Pedrosa was appointed artistic director of the museum. Speaking to <em><a href="https://www1.folha.uol.com.br/ilustrada/2026/07/estou-pronto-para-ir-embora-nao-tenho-apego-diz-heitor-martins-presidente-do-masp.shtml?utm_source=sharenativo&amp;utm_medium=social&amp;utm_campaign=sharenativo">Folha de S.Paulo</a></em>, Martins said Pedrosa<strong>’</strong>s future <strong>‘</strong>will depend on whoever succeeds me. At the same time&#8230; I don&#8217;t see any pressing need for a change of artistic director.<strong>’</strong></p>

<p><strong>Considering</strong> <strong>Agnes Scherer’s <em>Three Wicked Games</em> <strong>at Salzburger Kunstverein</strong>, Olga Hohmann wonders who gets to be part of the inner circle</strong></p>



<p><em>‘A human only plays when they are, in the full sense of the word, a human being, and they are only fully a human being when they play.’ </em><br>–– <em>Friedrich Schiller, </em>On the Aesthetic Education of Man<em> (1795)</em></p>



<p>Again and again, I catch sight of the two groups of figures from the doorway. They look tall and form a constellation, so self-contained, so absorbed in themselves and in one another, that I feel reluctant to disturb them. One group forms a closed circle; the other leaves it open. I am not sure I feel invited to join any of them.&nbsp;</p>



<p>I spontaneously think of my behavioural therapist, who discharged me after only a few sessions but left me with an intriguing piece of trivia: the so-called Zeigarnik effect. A drawn circle remains in memory when it has not been completed. An open circle haunts us in a way a closed circle does not. This theory, which refers to a concrete experimental setup in which patients literally had to draw circles on a piece of paper, can, of course, function as a metaphor for uncompleted tasks or&nbsp;<em>finding closure&nbsp;</em>in a social constellation. Yet my friend A. once said: “Strangely, I become nervous when the circle is closed, not when it is open.”&nbsp;</p>



<p>Open or closed, the circles behind the doorway haunt me, just like the empty-yet-animated gazes of the larger-than-life puppets – humanoid sculptures – that form them.</p>



<p>The sculptures seem almost to float in their fragility, while remaining stable, certain of themselves and of one another but aloof at the same time. They are made of paper and semitransparent fabric, which gives them a ghostlike quality, like a mirage in the desert, threatening to disappear if you come too close. Though of course they do not need to be observed to exist. Again and again I consider stepping among them, and again and again I abandon the thought. ‘The inner circle,’ I think. I have never liked exclusivity, yet it remains a determining force within the field that I navigate professionally. It constitutes relationality by introducing us to a concept of affiliation and distinction. ‘Where do I belong? Where – and with whom – do I stand? Against whom?’ Inclusion and exclusion seem to be not only aesthetic but political values within the artworld. The circle becomes a powerful figure. It is charged with the fantasy that there exists a group into which one might one day be admitted. This fantasy is structured as a game of desire that can never be fulfilled. What sustains desire is not admission itself but the expectation of admission – an endless game of ‘edging’.&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/13-Agnes-Scherer-1230x1844.png" alt="" class="wp-image-125797" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/13-Agnes-Scherer-1230x1844.png 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/13-Agnes-Scherer-600x900.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/13-Agnes-Scherer-300x450.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/13-Agnes-Scherer-768x1151.png 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/13-Agnes-Scherer-1025x1536.png 1025w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/13-Agnes-Scherer.png 1334w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Agnes Scherer,<em> Three Wicked Games</em>, 2026 (installation view, Salzburger Kunstverein). Photo: kunst-dokumentation.com</figcaption></figure>



<p>In Agnes Scherer’s exhibition&nbsp;<em>Three Wicked Games</em>&nbsp;at the Salzburger Kunstverein, the floor on which the figures seem to float is covered with paper depicting the surface of water. On the one hand you might recognise this as the type of setup used to protect a floor during a renovation; on the other you might feel like Jesus. Moreover, the painted floor in combination with the protagonists (whose features are drawn on) turn the whole room into one big painting. A painting that you are allowed to enter. You become part of the work, through your somatic presence alone. In doing so, you inevitably participate in the ‘wicked game’ of belonging and exclusion – whether you wish to or not. Coming closer to the figures, you are able to read the elaborately drawn signs they carry on their clothes, referring to expensive skin-care brands, for example; the viewer feels pleased to be able to detect and read these signifiers, understanding the mockery as an insider joke. Both the figures and we, the viewers, are thus trapped in the game of distinction.</p>



<p>Yet the circle evokes more than social hierarchy. It also suggests ritual, séance and childhood play. It recalls those games in which children stand in a circle while an unseen figure moves around them. “Dreh dich nicht um” (Don’t turn around), they chant, warning one another. The circle becomes a space of suspense, complicity and latent threat.</p>



<p>Friedrich Schiller understood that every game contains a seriousness of its own. A game consists not only of rules but of the collective decision to treat those rules as meaningful, binding. We know they are invented, yet we follow them as if they are laws. Refusing the rules means refusing the other players. The game only functions because everyone agrees to believe in its rules. It is an early form of social contract.</p>



<p>Games model social life because they teach us how relations are negotiated, constructed and maintained. A game is never ‘just’ a game – it is always a mirror of society. And as experience shows, one becomes a social outsider if one does not know the rules or does not take them seriously. ‘Not allowed to play’ is a social punishment.&nbsp;</p>



<p>These issues are already present in the works that are named as references in the text that accompanies the exhibition: Francisco Goya’s paintings&nbsp;<em>Blind Man’s Bluff</em>&nbsp;(1789) and&nbsp;<em>The Straw Manikin&nbsp;</em>(1791). The former features a group of well-dressed courtly characters dancing in a circle while a blindfolded youth in the middle tries to touch them with a spoon. The latter features four young women who each hold one corner of a sheet of cloth, which they use to toss and catch the titular straw doll. Both are commissions that the painter developed at the Spanish Court. When I encounter these references, I hesitate. I feel as though I have seen the motifs of the paintings before, albeit in a very different form.&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3-Agnes-Scherer-1230x1844.png" alt="" class="wp-image-125785" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3-Agnes-Scherer-1230x1844.png 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3-Agnes-Scherer-600x900.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3-Agnes-Scherer-300x450.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3-Agnes-Scherer-768x1151.png 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3-Agnes-Scherer-1025x1536.png 1025w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/3-Agnes-Scherer.png 1334w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Agnes Scherer,<em> Three Wicked Games</em>, 2026 (installation view, Salzburger Kunstverein). Photo: kunst-dokumentation.com</figcaption></figure>



<p>Eventually I recall a trip to Madrid where I unexpectedly encountered a complete set of Goya’s etching series&nbsp;<em>The Follies&nbsp;</em>(1815–23). The series depicts people absorbed in games and rituals. But unlike in Goya’s earlier works, which often feature members of the bourgeoisie or courtly elite, here we see figures that belong to the marginalised, the abandoned and the excluded. They may be<em>&nbsp;</em>society’s outcasts, but they appear to be playing the very same games played at court in&nbsp;<em>Blind Man’s Bluff</em>.</p>



<p>Unlike the elegant participants of&nbsp;<em>Blind Man’s Bluff</em>, the figures of&nbsp;<em>The Follies</em>&nbsp;appear unruly, autonomous, as if the same game operates a more radical mode of existence beyond the boundaries of social convention: the aristocrats appear controlled and distant, as representatives of their class; the figures in&nbsp;<em>The Follies</em>&nbsp;emerge as individuals, as protagonists. They seem animated by genuine pleasure: you instinctively want to join them, rather than the aristocrats.</p>



<p>This becomes especially revealing in relation to&nbsp;<em>Blind Man’s Bluff.&nbsp;</em>The painting can be read as an allegory of how the aristocrats move ‘blindly’ through society, fulfilling and performing the roles assigned to them. The game thus becomes more than a scene of leisure; it functions as a metaphor for the mechanisms of social conformity and obedience.</p>



<p>The distinction between those with agency and those without it is useful when thinking about Scherer’s installation. Her figures oscillate between personhood and puppethood. They are human enough to invite identification yet artificial enough to remain unsettling. Their circles – open or closed – are neither fully welcoming nor entirely forbidding.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/8-Agnes-Scherer-1230x820.png" alt="" class="wp-image-125787" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/8-Agnes-Scherer-1230x820.png 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/8-Agnes-Scherer-600x400.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/8-Agnes-Scherer-300x200.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/8-Agnes-Scherer-768x512.png 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/8-Agnes-Scherer-1536x1025.png 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/8-Agnes-Scherer.png 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Agnes Scherer,<em> Three Wicked Games</em>, 2026 (installation view, Salzburger Kunstverein). Photo: kunst-dokumentation.com</figcaption></figure>



<p>Standing on the paper-covered floor of the Salzburger Kunstverein I begin to wonder: who is the straw manikin and who is the blindfolded player today? Who is blind, and to what? Are we all playing blind man’s bluff?<em>&nbsp;</em>And above all: who gains entry into the ‘inner circle’, and who does not? Who wishes to enter which circle here?</p>



<p>The question of blindness leads naturally to Freud’s concept of the uncanny, which concerns itself with the invisible aspects of a seemingly transparent social reality. The uncanny (<em>das Unheimliche</em>) emerges when something is both familiar (<em>heimelig</em>) and strange, foreign, secret (<em>heimlich</em>) at the same time. Scherer’s figures produce precisely this effect.</p>



<p>These uncanny figures do not need my attention. The circle would continue to exist without me. The game would be played in my absence. I am not invited anyway.&nbsp;</p>



<p>And so I remain standing in the doorway. The figures continue their silent game. What lingers is not the certainty of belonging but the persistence of the desire to belong.</p>



<p>And with it, a final question: at what point does the (serious) game finally end?</p>



<p><em>Olga Hohmann is a writer and performer from Berlin, who is using text both a form of art and as a medium to discuss and accompany art.</em></p>
</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[Dubel Art Prize 2025/26 Announces Winner]]></title><description><![CDATA[The annual award supports emerging British artists through a yearlong programme of exhibitions and events]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/dubel-art-prize-2025-26-announces-winner/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/dubel-art-prize-2025-26-announces-winner/</guid><pubDate>Wed, 05 Aug 2026 11:06:11 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<p><strong>The annual award supports emerging British artists through a yearlong programme of exhibitions and events</strong></p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ellie-Damant-Prize-Winner-speech-2026-1230x1230.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-126010" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ellie-Damant-Prize-Winner-speech-2026-1230x1230.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ellie-Damant-Prize-Winner-speech-2026-600x600.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ellie-Damant-Prize-Winner-speech-2026-300x300.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ellie-Damant-Prize-Winner-speech-2026-768x768.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ellie-Damant-Prize-Winner-speech-2026-1536x1536.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Ellie-Damant-Prize-Winner-speech-2026.jpg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Ellie Damant accepts the 2025/26 Dubel Art Prize</figcaption></figure>



<p>Earlier this year, Ellie Damant was named winner of the 2025/26 <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://dubelprize.com/" target="_blank">Dubel Art Prize</a>. The annual award supports emerging British artists through a yearlong programme of exhibitions and events, before a judging panel selects its Emerging Artist of the Year. Alongside a £20,000 award, the winner receives exhibition, publishing and gallery opportunities intended to support the development and visibility of their practice. Trained in fine art and human anatomy at Oxford, Damant uses painting as a form of inquiry, examining how identity, meaning and value are constructed, with recent work focusing on money and commodification.</p>



<p><strong>ArtReview</strong> <em>Why do barcodes appear so often in your work, and what drew you to them as a symbol of exchange?</em></p>



<p><strong>Ellie Damant</strong> Scanning a barcode reminds me of the ‘phantom-like’ value Marx describes in <em>Das Kapital</em> (1867), which fleetingly appears. So capturing ‘value’, visually, manifested as a barcode imprinted onto a face, as in <em>B Priceless</em> (2022): it’s a form of resistance from inside the system, signalling a priceless quality precisely because it is on a unique human individual. I began painting barcodes across my own face as <em>Le Gal Tender,</em> a performance character who mirrors the polarity of bull/bear markets. From there the barcode became a recurring lens for examining social/monetary power across different systems and figures, always haunting the image.</p>



<p><strong>AR</strong> <em>You have described painting as a form of philosophy. How do you prevent the philosophical ideas behind a work from becoming too illustrative or didactic?</em></p>



<p><strong>ED </strong>When I take established philosophical positions and aesthetic conventions, part of the process of reinventing these is to contort them by testing their limits. I aim for the clarity of the image to contrast with the instability of the ideas. By placing extremes of wealth, power, voice or the present and infinite in the same frame, I leave space for viewers to decide where they stand, or to reject the spectrum altogether. In the landscape painting <em>…But Eternity Cannot Be Sold </em>(2024) I paint the phrase ‘money is time’ in market ticker tape across the top of the canvas. The painting sets the human idea that time equals money against the sky’s reply: ‘but eternity cannot be sold’. A viewer can decide how they value their own time, perhaps choosing resistance to either polarity with their response. In <em>Plato’s Code</em> (2025) I began with the allegory of Plato’s cave and approached it through Merleau-Ponty’s emphasis on bodily experience as a ground of truth. In this painting, Stonehenge casts a shadow that becomes a barcode on a phone screen; this is to contrast an ancient world without this technology with the profit-driven distortions of the present, while also recalling that trade itself has ancient origins. When looking at this painting we see it as a mediated image via a phone, an almost ubiquitous experience now. This places the viewer in the position of reflecting on the nature of reality for them, and also our collective contemporary online experience through these devices.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Platos-Code-2025-1230x1226.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-126013" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Platos-Code-2025-1230x1226.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Platos-Code-2025-600x598.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Platos-Code-2025-300x299.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Platos-Code-2025-768x766.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Platos-Code-2025-1536x1531.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Platos-Code-2025.jpg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption><em>Plato’s Code</em>, 2025. Courtesy the artist</figcaption></figure>



<p><strong>AR</strong> <em>Figures including Kim Kardashian, Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk appear in your paintings as contemporary icons of value and power. What led you to choosing these individuals in particular and what makes portraiture a useful way of examining the systems they represent?</em></p>



<p><strong>ED</strong> Each of these figures represents a different form of contemporary power. Kardashian turns visibility and the curated self into economic force; Zuckerberg’s platforms represent one of the most extensive monetisations of personal data; Musk embodies a scale of wealth and influence almost without historical precedent. Together they personify systems of visibility, data extraction and technological influence. By combining symbolic and art-historical visual languages, the portrait can operate simultaneously as representation, icon, satire and philosophical proposition, leaving the contradictions open for the viewer.</p>



<p><strong>AR</strong> <em>Your paintings often borrow from religious art and art history. What interests you about placing contemporary figures within those traditions?</em></p>



<p><strong>ED</strong> What interests me is that these traditions and the contemporary value-creation systems of social media and celebrity culture all participate in meaning construction. Placing a contemporary figure inside older visual languages lets me compare and challenge the different systems contemporaneously. In <em>Salvator Verbi Liberae (Saviour of Free Speech)</em> (2025), Elon Musk replaces the figure in Leonardo’s <em>Salvator Mundi </em>(c.1499–1510), linking the richest living individual with the most expensive painting ever sold. The frame references Musk’s purchase of Twitter, while a barcoded planet Mars appears as an absurdist commodity in the corner. The work examines how extreme wealth reshapes structures of value creation.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Golden-Kim-Esse-Est-Percipi2025-1230x1234.jpeg" alt="" class="wp-image-126015" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Golden-Kim-Esse-Est-Percipi2025-1230x1234.jpeg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Golden-Kim-Esse-Est-Percipi2025-600x602.jpeg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Golden-Kim-Esse-Est-Percipi2025-300x301.jpeg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Golden-Kim-Esse-Est-Percipi2025-768x770.jpeg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Golden-Kim-Esse-Est-Percipi2025-1531x1536.jpeg 1531w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Golden-Kim-Esse-Est-Percipi2025.jpeg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption><em>Golden Kim (Esse Est Percipi)</em>, 2025. Courtesy the artist</figcaption></figure>



<p><strong>AR</strong> <em>Are you interested in what has replaced religion as a source of belief and meaning?</em></p>



<p><strong>ED </strong>Religion being replaced remains debatable. What interests me is the almost religious devotion of current consumer culture. Brands seek value through celebrity endorsement, attaching a celebrity’s aura to commodities rather than arguing for their commodity’s quality. Influencers function like saints. In <em>Golden Kim (Esse Est Percipi) </em>(2025), the gold background places Kim Kardashian within the visual tradition of icons. The work is named after George Berkeley’s claim that ‘to be is to be perceived’, an observation he made in the eighteenth century that feels newly pointed in a culture where social media can make invisibility feel close to non-existence.</p>



<p><strong>AR</strong> <em>How have social media and digital technology changed the way we understand value, identity and power?</em></p>



<p><strong>ED</strong> Social media began as a community of sharing but has become more extractive. What concerns me is the concentration of power in a few companies that map, predict and shape behaviour before conscious choice is made. What’s at stake is individual agency. Mark Zuckerberg in <em>Own Thyself (Temet Nosce – Know Thyself) </em>(2025) appears as a figure wherein this new frontier of data control is concentrated, a frontier that will increasingly shape democracy and freedom. The work sets data ownership against individual sovereignty, leaving the tension unresolved.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/The-End-Is-Buy-2025-1230x1230.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-126001" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/The-End-Is-Buy-2025-1230x1230.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/The-End-Is-Buy-2025-600x600.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/The-End-Is-Buy-2025-300x300.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/The-End-Is-Buy-2025-768x768.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/The-End-Is-Buy-2025-1536x1536.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/The-End-Is-Buy-2025.jpg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption><em>The End Is Buy</em>, 2025. Courtesy the artist</figcaption></figure>



<p><strong>AR</strong> <em>Humour and wordplay run through titles such as </em>The End Is Buy<em> and </em>Consumer<em>. What role do they play in the work?</em></p>



<p><strong>ED </strong>Humour and wordplay layer contradictory meanings while leaving space for playful new interpretations and associations. In <em>The End Is Buy </em>(2025), the phrase ‘the end is nigh’ becomes a joke about consumption. Magritte, one of the highest-selling artists of the twentieth century, is drawn into the visual pun, while the bird-man and aurochs from Lascaux recall human origins and, for me, the possibility that art and belief offer a third way through the dilemma of life and death. <em>Consumer</em> is darker. The serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer’s consumption of bodies is contrasted with a consumer culture that demands infinite growth from finite resources. In this painting the police height chart actually presents the statistics of the National Readership Survey’s social consumer grades.</p>



<p><strong>AR</strong> <em>How will winning the Dubel Prize affect what you make next?</em></p>



<p><strong>ED</strong> Winning the prize has given the work a wider platform and focused attention. It helps confirm that my exploration of markets, digital systems, value, belief, power and embodiment resonates beyond the studio.</p>



<p>My next works will extend the enquiry into questions of truth, justice, systems of power, money and value. I expect to abstract and evolve further value symbols and continue using poetry as I have in <em>Everything I Ever Wanted Is Here Before My Eyes</em> (2025). The philosophical method will remain central: a dialectical approach allowing new ideas to emerge through the process of painting, so layered meanings can form in conversation with the viewer.</p>

<p>Valerie Hillings has been appointed as inaugural director of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, set to open in <a href="https://artreview.com/guggenheim-abu-dhabi-announces-opening-date/">December this year</a>, the Abu Dhabi Department of Culture and Tourism has announced. </p>



<p>Hillings has been closely involved with the project during its development, serving as the Guggenheim Foundation’s curator and associate director of curatorial affairs for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi from 2009 to 2018, working on collection strategy and acquisitions and on pre-opening programming. Courtesy Lubov, New York</figcaption></figure>



<p>Francisco Correa Cordero, who founded New York’s Lubov gallery, has died. The 37-year-old’s death was described as peaceful. </p>



<p>The gallery, which Cordero opened in Chinatown in 2017, represented a small group of artists, but has staged shows with many more. A recent exhibition by My Barbarian, the group’s first since a Whitney Museum solo show, featured work that ‘celebrate(s) queer, leftist agency’, <a href="https://artreview.com/my-barbarian-cat-suit-review/">Louis Bury wrote in <em>ArtReview</em></a>. Painter Kane Huynh is due to have an exhibition at the gallery in the Autumn. </p>



<p>The gallery’s roster features Theodore Darst, Bryce Kroll, Marsha Pels, Connor Marie Stankard and Harry Tafoya. Previously artists including Jenna Westra, Victor Boullet and pairings of Andres Serrano and Benjamin Bertocci, Jon Rafman and Parker Ito, have shown at the space. </p>



<p>Born in Mexico, Cordero came to the US to study photography at the School of Visual Arts, taking jobs and organising shows at Yancey Richardson Gallery, Martos Gallery, Aperture, Humble Arts Foundation, the Richard Avedon Foundation and Exit Art. </content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[Ellen Pau: Less Than Meets the Eye]]></title><description><![CDATA[Though these works might resonate with certain experiences of Hong Kong’s recent past, they’re far from political commentary]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/ellen-pau-she-moves-sculpturecenter-new-york-review-marcus-civin/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/ellen-pau-she-moves-sculpturecenter-new-york-review-marcus-civin/</guid><pubDate>Tue, 04 Aug 2026 10:24:58 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<p><strong>Though these works might resonate with certain experiences of Hong Kong’s recent past, they’re far from political commentary</strong></p>



<p>Ellen Pau’s career survey at SculptureCenter is not as political as the circumstances in Hong Kong under which her work emerged – during the 1980s and 90s, between the signing of the Sino-British Joint Declaration and the 1997 handover – might suggest. Take the modest but charming single-channel black-and-white video <em>Operation Theatre</em> (1995), which plays on a monitor mounted high on the wall in the first gallery, as though part of a surveillance system. Semitransparent hospital workers and patients pass through a hallway, their forms rendered ghostlike, evoking the bleary-eyed vision associated with fever or illness in this gently altered but otherwise quotidian fragment. Similarly, <em>She Moves</em> (1988) – the earliest work in the exhibition and a quintessential example of video installation in the golden age of the form – is a wall-size projection showing raindrops sliding down a window. The projection is flanked by sheer curtains; a radio on the gallery floor next to an empty chair blasts the cloying 1939 British ballad <em>We’ll Meet Again</em>. Here and now, the song’s promise of reunion becomes less a foreboding allegory for the authoritarian rule eventually imposed on Hong Kongers by the Chinese government and more of an ironic soundtrack to sentimental wallowing. Though these works present psychological states that might resonate with or stand adjacent to certain experiences of Hong Kong’s recent past – waiting, being watched and grieving – they are, just in themselves, far from political commentary. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-1230x923.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125852" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-1230x923.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-600x450.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-300x225.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-768x576.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_129.jpg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption><em>Pledge: Bik Lai Chu 碧麗珠, 1993/2018</em>, installation view. Photo: Charles Benton. Courtesy the artist, SculptureCenter, New York and Kiang Malingue, Hong Kong, New York</figcaption></figure>



<p><em>Pledge: Bik Lai Chu</em> (1993/2018) – one of Pau’s best-known works – and <em>Pledge: I Can Only Tell It to Strangers</em> (1996/2018) both deploy video recordings of Pau hunched on the ground in her underwear, rhythmically striking her head against the underside of a dressing table. Curators and critics have pointed out that the word ‘pledge’ here refers to both a popular line of cleaning products and China’s promise to maintain Hong Kong’s pre-handover freedoms, but if indeed Pau is simultaneously hitting her head against patriarchy and broken political promises, the titles are doing a lot of heavy lifting. The same could be said for <em>The Great Movement: Red Stock</em> (1996/2018), a digital projection of a nearly lifeless hand blocking a passageway in SculptureCenter’s mazelike basement. The title refers to China making shares of state-funded companies available on the Hong Kong stock exchange and the territory’s dependence on the resulting capital influx, but the hand alone doesn’t convey what the exhibition guide describes as ‘a sense of foreboding’ related to the economic situation. It just hangs there.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-1230x923.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125851" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-1230x923.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-600x450.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-300x225.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-768x576.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SC_May26_068.jpg 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption><em>Where Have All the Flowers Gone 冇花 冇假</em>, 2026, installation view. Photo: Charles Benton. Courtesy the artist and SculptureCenter, New York</figcaption></figure>



<p>One of the newest and least resolved works in the exhibition, <em>Where Have All the Flowers Gone</em> (2026), is unmistakably bland and unfortunately so, right when the artworld is starting to pay attention to Pau’s long-term dedication to experimental video as an artist and curator. Evoking vigils and protests, its centrepiece, an enlarged candlelike form, displays a three-dimensional video flame that flares when viewers approach. Nearby, two common dinner plates feature thinly decorative designs generated by spinning a representation of the bauhinia, an orchid that serves as Hong Kong’s primary symbol, appearing on currency, on the regional flag and at pro-democracy demonstrations. The works engender none of the fear, exhilaration or solidarity of vigils or protests. At best, they resemble souvenirs from these events.</p>



<p><strong><em>Ellen Pau: </em>She Moves<em> at SculptureCenter, New York, <a rel="noreferrer noopener" href="https://www.sculpture-center.org/exhibitions/14802/ellen-pau-she-moves" target="_blank">28 May – 16 August</a></em></strong></p>

</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[Im Youngzoo: Requiem for Technological Progress]]></title><description><![CDATA[A recent exhibition suggests that our drive to develop new technologies indicates a spiritual need to manage ‘existential uncertainty’]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/im-youngzoo-the-late-review-jenny-wu/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/im-youngzoo-the-late-review-jenny-wu/</guid><pubDate>Mon, 03 Aug 2026 11:31:30 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<p><strong>A recent exhibition suggests that our drive to develop new technologies indicates a spiritual need to manage ‘existential uncertainty’</strong></p>



<p>This dense, heady show by Seoul-based artist Im Youngzoo is anchored by an hour-long, seven-channel video installation. Dispersed throughout the first gallery (of two), including a triptych of screens looming overhead and on a tombstone-like vertical monitor, <em>The Late&nbsp;故</em>&nbsp;(2025–26) follows scattered acts – a figure in a white Ghillie suit romping around in the snow, a woman receiving acupuncture on the crown of her head, a self-driving car navigating country roads, people visiting the cemetery – that sum up to what could be called, per one set of intertitles, a ‘survival report’, ‘a final witness’. While the seemingly disconnected scenes progress, typed texts scroll by. They include emails, weather updates, hypnosis prompts, stray thoughts about death and, in particular, questions about those who play dead.</p>



<p>A survival tactic shared by animals, as well as, the onscreen text points out, human organs (as in the case of hypometabolism) and machines (such as when a computer ‘halts its operation’ instead of opting for a ‘faulty execution’), playing dead is something visitors to Im’s exhibition can test out for themselves. In the centre of the first gallery is a long, stony grey platform. On it lies what appears to be a foil-covered corpse in a VR headset (<em>The Late VR</em>, 2025–26). But the platform also offers a niche for the not-yet-dead: to watch Im’s single-channel video<em> One Hundred Meeting Point</em> (2025–26), you withdraw into this single-occupancy alcove and stretch out on your back. A monitor on the ceiling inside plays animations starring an acupuncture dummy and a Buddha statue, with spooky footage of someone with a flashlight approaching you on a dark road. Other videos installed in cubicles on either end of the platform – such as <em>Waiting M</em> (2021), which collages, among other curiosities, footage from Mars with meditations on Soviet scientist Alexander Chizhevsky’s theories linking solar cycles to financial crises and political revolutions – invite viewers to kneel like mourners.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-1230x923.png" alt="" class="wp-image-123849" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-1230x923.png 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-600x450.png 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-300x225.png 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-768x576.png 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella-1536x1152.png 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/The-Late-2026-installation-view-Photo-Jason-Mandella.png 2000w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Im Youngzoo, <i>The Late 故</i>, 2026 (installation view, Space ZeroOne, New York). Photo: Jason Mandella</figcaption></figure>



<p>As a whole, the show suggests that the applied sciences – pseudo and otherwise – and humankind’s drive to develop new technologies – for image capture, remote sensing, creating virtual realities and so on – arise out of a spiritual need to manage what the exhibition handout calls ‘existential uncertainty’. For nations, this angst might manifest as a technological arms race, and Im hints at ways in which governments, like South Korea’s starting in the latter half of the twentieth century, fuelled various tech frenzies, with mixed results. In the second gallery, whose walls are bathed in antiseptic yellow-green light, copies of a 1,254-page artist book, also titled <em>The Late&nbsp;故</em>&nbsp;– are displayed on a wooden platform. Here, Im writes, for instance, that when Korean president Lee Myung-bak proposed his ‘747 Plan’ during his 2007 campaign – a plan to increase the country’s GDP and per capita income, and transform it into the seventh largest economy in the world – ‘VR was tapped as a core technology in the strategy’. ‘The Ministry of Science and Technology announced an investment of one trillion won to “take the first place in the global VR market by 2015,”’ Im writes. ‘But with the Lehman Brothers’ bankruptcy in September 2008, the global financial crisis annulled all such ambitions.’ In view of this, <em>The Late VR</em> increasingly resembles not a wake for a headset-addicted human but a requiem for technological progress itself.</p>



<p>Then again, our devices don’t really die, even when they’ve outlived their potential. Opposite the platform in the second gallery stands <em>A Dark Room</em> (2025–26), three broken vertical monitors, and a further functioning one, mounted side by side like panels of a folding screen. Those that are switched on display haunting images, like the skirt and feet of a floating woman. Others offer nothing, until one notices the words of caution – ‘Beware of ghosts’, ‘Beware of science’ – smudged in Korean on their mirror-smooth surfaces. Maybe, Im’s clues suggest, some technologies are simply playing dead – withdrawing from us, transforming from coveted tools into vessels for our fears and longings, objects we in turn revere and contemplate.</p>



<p><strong>Im Youngzoo: The Late 故 <em>is on view at Space ZeroOne, New York though 25 July</em></strong></p>

</content:encoded></item><item><title><![CDATA[‘The Savage Landscape: How We Made the Wilderness’ by Cal Flyn, Reviewed]]></title><description><![CDATA[Does any true wilderness still exist on this earth?]]></description><link>https://artreview.com/the-savage-landscape-by-cal-flyn-review-oliver-basciano/</link><guid isPermaLink="false">https://artreview.com/the-savage-landscape-by-cal-flyn-review-oliver-basciano/</guid><pubDate>Mon, 03 Aug 2026 08:59:48 GMT</pubDate><content:encoded>
<p><strong>Does any true wilderness still exist on this earth?</strong></p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-1230x922.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-123111" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-1230x922.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-600x450.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-300x225.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-768x576.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy-1536x1152.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Untitled-12-copy.jpg 1890w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /></figure>



<p>The central question of <em>The Savage Landscape</em> is whether any true ‘wilderness’ still exists on this earth. Wilderness in scare quotes because, Cal Flyn reflects, the term is defined by human absence, but is largely contingent on human action. As we approach a point at which every spot of land will be explored and mapped, those territories that remain truly wild – savage even – are few, their existence largely determined by the grace of humans. Even the deepest ocean bed is becoming subject to the cartographer, forever the precursor to the despoiler, Flyn points out.</p>



<p>This book documents the Scottish writer’s travels, from the Brazilian Amazon to the Sinai Desert, Antarctica to Iceland’s volcanoes; her sublime descriptions of some of the most remote places in the world are a joy in their own right, but Flyn undercuts the travelogue with difficult ethical dilemmas that give the book a powerful, tricksy, narrative. She asks us to consider, for example, the plight of the Batwa people, shut out from their own territory in Uganda by the government and global conservation charities, some of whose staff have been found to commit atrocities against them (in neighbouring DR Congo), in the name of protecting the bush pig, the jackal and, most famously thanks to Dian Fossey and the film <em>Gorillas in the Mist</em> (1988), the great apes who make the forests their home (Fossey too was known to assault and torture in her efforts to maintain the gorillas’ peace). Things get even more ethically murky when Flyn accompanies big-game hunters in Mozambique – queasy-making wealthy Westerners who pay thousands to shoot lions and the like – but whose bloodthirsty dollars provide the necessary funding to preserve fast swathes of forest and wider species. She interrogates her own bias too, noting that she often feels ‘hampered by my own scientific training, my habitual clutching at rational argument’, observing that some of the best-preserved terrains have been protected not by research and education but by the mythologies of their indigenous people. The <em>yulsa</em> spirits of the Nepalese Bon people have offered more light-touch protection to their mountainous territory than any number of NGOs or government military might.</p>



<p>It feels that any attempt to escape the Anthropocene’s curse is doomed to failure; though fear emerges as one possible antidote. Not of the hysterical kind, but a precolonial respect for the unknown, a fear of predators real and imagined. For Flyn, the irony not lost on the author, the age of human exploration and documentation has been our greatest triumph and the world’s great undoing.</p>

<p><strong>What if artistic innovation emerges from material itself, rather than being imposed on it?</strong></p>



<p>The components are simple: sod and a body. The grassy panels, laid carefully over a person underneath, begin to pulse. This is <a href="https://artreview.com/ar-april-2018-feature-ana-mendieta/">Ana Mendieta</a>’s <em>Grass Breathing </em>(1974), part of a group of performances, recorded on video, that demonstrate the late Cuban artist’s inventive approaches to her environment. <em>Grass Breathing</em> finds new company in this exhibition, which gathers contemporary, often Latinx or Indigenous American artists whose practices stretch Mendieta’s ideas into the twenty-first century, enlivening unpredictable natural materials in similarly unconventional ways. Their grouping, an opening wall text declares, ‘celebrates kinship through a shared aesthetic language rather than fostering an ethnographic gaze or a desire for cultural authenticity’. Some unifying ideas emerge, particularly around nature’s ephemerality and its formal dictates, but the divergent array of artworks on view eventually strays from the exhibition’s compelling concerns.</p>



<p>Diné artist <a href="https://artreview.com/raven-chacon-what-does-america-sound-like-right-now-geeta-dayal/">Raven Chacon</a>’s aural composition <em>Study for Vertical Earth </em>(2026) fills the foyer: a thunderous, bass-heavy score, the result of underground microphones recording subtle earthly movements. Multiple artworks made using rocks, stone and sand greet the viewer upon entry, in turn highlighting the sanitisation of most institutional spaces. <a href="https://artreview.com/edgar-calel-balabaj-jaguar-stone-sculpture-center-new-york-review/">Edgar Calel</a>’s room-size installation <em>Ch’ablin nu rayb’el Chua taj ab’ej </em>(Splashes of My Desire on Top of Stones, 2026) stages local sandstone and lava boulders among mountains of brown dirt, each rock adorned with ceremonial offerings: dried flowers, eucalyptus and the artist’s own oxidised blood. In the next gallery, Jackie Amézquita further deconstructs the visual language of the museum: <em>Cuerpos terrestres en fluidez </em>(Terrestrial Bodies of Fluidity, 2025–26) features the destroyed remains of two monolithic, columnal sculptures, now broken into small bricks that resemble crushed pedestals, as though the museum itself were an ancient ruin.</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-1230x692.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125737" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-1230x692.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-600x338.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-300x169.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-768x432.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023-1536x864.jpg 1536w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Hammer-2026-04-06_023.jpg 1600w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>(left) Carmen Argote, <em>an archetype of touch</em>, 2025, avocado, cochineal and lemon juice on paper, 457 x 244 cm; (right) Carmen Argote, <em>an archetype of stillness</em>, 2026, avocado, cochineal and lemon juice on paper, 488 x 244 cm. Courtesy the artist and Commonwealth Council, Los Angeles</figcaption></figure>



<p>Others deviate less from Western artistic forms but use volatile, restrictive materials – often naturally derived ones native to the Americas. Carmen Argote, in <em>an archetype of stillness </em>(2026) and <em>an archetype of touch </em>(2025), has drawn gestural floor-to-ceiling depictions of human bodies using avocado mashed into an oily pigment – a substance that gradually destroys the paper beneath. Indigenous Amazonian artist Nereyda López crafts strikingly emotive figurative sculptures from <em>chambira </em>palm tree branches; <em>Ta+fe/Sacharuna </em>(2019) transforms one tapered frond into an indignant, hoop-earringed figure, its convex shape curving to form a chin, jaw and forehead. In some cases, an artist’s unique materials are difficult to discern, but require subtle alterations to gallery display: Peruvian artist and cosmologist Santiago Yahuarcani applies colour extracted from local plants – similar in appearance to that of tempera or acrylic – to papery tree bark ‘canvases’ to make vivid narrative paintings that must be kept in low light to avoid damage (<em>Bufeos robando mujeres en la fiesta del yacuche </em>[Dolphins Abducting Women in the Festival of the Yacuche]<em>, </em>2022).</p>



<figure class="wp-block-image size-large"><img src="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-1230x1442.jpg" alt="" class="wp-image-125738" srcset="https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-1230x1442.jpg 1230w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-600x703.jpg 600w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-300x352.jpg 300w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-768x900.jpg 768w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09-1310x1536.jpg 1310w, https://backend.artreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Nereyda_09.jpg 1706w" sizes="(max-width: 1230px) 100vw, 1230px" /><figcaption>Nereyda Lopez, <em>Ta+fe / Sacharuna</em>, 2019, vegetable fibers and wood, 95 x 40 x 40 cm. Courtesy collection of Michael Krichman and Carmen Cuenca</figcaption></figure>



<p>Nature and climate change are recurring subjects, but not all works coherently engage these concerns at a formal level, particularly in later galleries. In Patricia Dominguez-Claro’s <em>Plant Saga </em>installation (2026), dried roses scatter decoratively, and incomprehensibly, alongside watercolour drawings of women and military drones. Others employ clay in order to explore personal history and experience, but this material choice feels incidental: Naomi Gamarra’s wall-hanging sculpture <em>Mirando arriba </em>(Looking Up, 2025) is an arched, decorative ceramic comb adorned with dangling clay lice, an eerie, if heavy-handed, exploration of ancient Peruvian bodily rituals and contemporary femininity that also feels out of place here. These works often deploy ancient ceramic techniques, but their methods have little influence on the results: Raven Halfmoon’s adjacent <em>Soku Sahyodahney’ah </em>(Caddo – Sun Twins, 2023) collages contemporary cultural signifiers with those of her Caddo Nation ancestry: two longhaired, conjoined ceramic figures – the ‘Sun Twins’ of Caddo origin stories – drip with graffitilike red and yellow colouring, the artist’s ‘tag’ scrawled across the back of their shared torso.</p>



<p>What’s most exciting about this exhibition is the idea that artistic innovation emerges from material itself, rather than being imposed on it – and that many sculptors, painters and ceramicists have long considered this challenge as more than a means to an end. But the energy present when I entered – lively chatter punctuated by Chacon’s guttural music – was not palpable as I exited through its final rooms, which overflowed with artworks that diverged from the exhibition’s earlier focus on material into explorations of identity instead. At best, <em>Several Eternities </em>vocalises the radical ‘shared aesthetic language’ of a growing force in contemporary art, but too often its inclusions dissolve into illegible survey.</p>



<p><strong>Several Eternities in a Day: Form in the Age of Living Materials</strong><em><strong> at Hammer Museum, Los Angeles, <a href="https://hammer.ucla.edu/exhibitions/2026/several-eternities-day-form-age-living-materials" target="_blank" rel="noreferrer noopener">5 April – 23 August</a></strong></em></p>
